slides.title: The anatomical map: CNS, PNS, and ENS
slides.memory: Central = control center. Peripheral = connecting paths. Enteric = intestine.
slides.source: Book pp. 390–392; C12 L1 slide 2; T-D.
slides.notes: The lecture often simplifies to central versus peripheral. The assigned book explicitly includes the ENS as a third anatomical division. Retain that textbook distinction when a question asks for all three.
content: CNS: Brain and spinal cord: integrate sensory input, process information, and coordinate motor commands.
PNS: Nervous tissue outside the CNS and ENS in this textbook’s framing. Cranial and spinal nerves connect the CNS with peripheral tissues.
ENS: Neuronal networks in the digestive-tract walls. Can coordinate local visceral reflexes; sympathetic and parasympathetic activity influence them.
BIG DISTINCTION: Anatomical divisions describe structures. Functional divisions describe what information travels through those structures.

slides.title: Afferent arrives; efferent exits
slides.memory: SAME: Sensory–Afferent; Motor–Efferent. “A arrives, E exits.”
slides.source: Book pp. 390–391, 395; C12 L1 slide 2; T-B/T-C.
slides.notes: Do not equate somatic with always voluntary. A patellar reflex still uses skeletal muscle and therefore is somatic. Both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions belong on the motor side of this introductory map.
content: AFFERENT / SENSORY: Receptors send information toward the CNS: special senses, somatic sensation, and visceral sensation.
EFFERENT / MOTOR: Commands leave the CNS for effectors. “Motor” includes muscles and glands—not just visible movement.
SOMATIC MOTOR: Targets skeletal muscle. Includes voluntary movement and involuntary somatic reflexes.
AUTONOMIC MOTOR: Targets smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands, and adipose tissue. Sympathetic and parasympathetic are its major divisions.

slides.title: Neuron anatomy: trace the signal
slides.memory: Dendrites receive; axon carries; terminals communicate.
slides.source: Book pp. 392–393, 409; C12 L1 slides 3–4; T-C.
slides.notes: Nissl bodies are clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes, involved in protein synthesis. Mitochondria supply ATP. Neurofilaments and neurotubules support the cell. Mature CNS neurons are generally long-lived and have high metabolic demand; the book notes limited neural stem-cell exceptions to the usual inability to divide.
content: INPUT REGION: Dendrites receive information. The cell body is the soma; the perikaryon is its cytoplasm around the nucleus.
TRIGGER REGION: Axon hillock is the transition from soma to axon. The initial segment is the key action-potential initiation region in the chapter’s model.
CONDUCTING REGION: Axon carries the action potential. Axolemma = axon membrane; axoplasm = axon cytoplasm.
OUTPUT REGION: Collaterals branch along an axon. Telodendria are fine terminal branches ending in synaptic terminals.

slides.title: Axonal transport: supply line and return route
slides.memory: Kinesin keeps going out; dynein delivers back.
slides.source: Book p. 393; C12 L1 slide 3.
slides.notes: The rabies clinical note uses retrograde axonal transport to explain how material entering peripheral terminals can reach the CNS. Transport of cellular cargo is not the same thing as propagation of an action potential.
content: ANTEROGRADE: Kinesin carries material away from the cell body toward terminals along neurotubules.
RETROGRADE: Dynein carries material from terminals back toward the cell body.
ENERGY + SPEED: Transport uses ATP. The book gives fast transport up to 1,000 mm/day, averaging about 300; slow transport is a few mm/day.
WHY IT MATTERS: Terminals need proteins, enzymes and vesicle materials. Retrograde transport also returns debris and can carry harmful material toward the CNS.

slides.title: Four neuron shapes
slides.memory: BI = two processes. MULTI = many dendrites. UNI = one main process.
slides.source: Book pp. 394–395; C12 L1 slide 5; T-B/T-C.
slides.notes: Source caution: the lecture groups three examples as sensory and multipolar as motor, while also acknowledging interneurons can look multipolar. Use the example classification for the lecture diagram, but do not memorize “every multipolar neuron is motor.”
content: ANAXONIC: Many processes but no obvious axon; found in the brain and special sense organs in the textbook.
BIPOLAR: One dendrite and one axon, with the soma between them; associated with special senses.
UNIPOLAR: A single process with the soma off to the side; typical sensory neurons of the PNS.
MULTIPOLAR: Many dendrites and one axon. Includes skeletal motor neurons and many CNS neurons; shape alone does not prove a motor function.

slides.title: The two PNS glia—and the myelin comparison
slides.memory: Schwann = peripheral sheath; oligodendrocyte = central, multiple segments.
slides.source: Book pp. 398–400; C12 L1 slides 6, 9; T-A/T-C.
content: SATELLITE CELLS: Surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia and regulate their local chemical environment.
SCHWANN CELLS: Enclose peripheral axons. A myelinating Schwann cell forms one internode on one axon; many cells cover the full length.
OLIGODENDROCYTES: A CNS oligodendrocyte sends processes to myelinate segments of multiple axons.
UNMYELINATED ≠ UNPROTECTED: A Schwann cell can enclose several unmyelinated axons without winding a thick myelin sheath around them.

slides.title: Myelin, nodes, gray matter and white matter
slides.memory: White = wires; gray = processing groups. These are helpful summaries, not exclusive contents.
slides.source: Book pp. 398–400, 440; C12 L1 slides 7–9; T-A.
slides.notes: Neurolemma is the outer Schwann-cell surface around a peripheral axon. Gray and white matter also contain neuroglia; neither is literally only one component.
content: MYELIN: Lipid-rich membrane wrapping that electrically insulates axon segments and increases propagation speed.
INTERNODE / NODE: Internode = myelinated segment. Node of Ranvier = gap between internodes where action potentials are regenerated.
WHITE MATTER: Rich in myelinated axons; organized mainly for moving information between locations.
GRAY MATTER: Rich in cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated processes; important for integration. In the cord it forms the central butterfly.

slides.title: Peripheral repair: degeneration comes before regrowth
slides.memory: Break down → clean up → guide → regrow → reconnect.
slides.source: Book pp. 399–401, 442; C12 L1 slide 10; T-A.
slides.notes: Source caution: the handout loosely labels Wallerian degeneration as the regeneration process. The book distinguishes degeneration of the distal segment from subsequent repair. CNS repair is much more limited: many axons are involved, astrocytic scar tissue can obstruct growth, and inhibitory chemicals can impede regrowth.
content: 1 | DISTAL BREAKDOWN: After severe axon injury, the disconnected distal axon and its myelin degenerate: Wallerian degeneration.
2 | CLEANUP + GUIDE: Macrophages remove debris. Schwann cells proliferate and form a guiding cord.
3 | AXON REGROWTH: The surviving neuron can send sprouts into that pathway; Schwann cells enclose the regrowing axon.
4 | FUNCTIONAL OUTCOME: Recovery depends on regrowth reaching the correct target. Misalignment, a large gap or failure to reconnect can prevent recovery.

slides.title: Resting membrane potential: start at about −70 mV
slides.memory: Na+ mainly outside; K+ mainly inside; inside is negative at rest.
slides.source: Book pp. 402–405; C12 L2 slides 1–5; T-A/T-B.
content: WHAT IS MEASURED?: The voltage inside the cell relative to outside—not an absolute amount of electricity in the cell.
ION DISTRIBUTION: Na+ is high outside; K+ is high inside. Intracellular negatively charged proteins also matter.
SELECTIVE PERMEABILITY: At rest, the membrane is more permeable to K+ than Na+. Leak channels remain open.
POLARIZED: A resting neuron has a charge separation and can respond to a stimulus; it is not currently firing an action potential.

slides.title: The sodium–potassium pump: 3 out, 2 in, 1 ATP
slides.memory: “3 Na out, 2 K in, 1 ATP.” Say the direction every time.
slides.source: Book pp. 403, 405, 412; C12 L2 slides 1–5; T-A–T-D.
slides.notes: The book explicitly says many action potentials can occur before bulk ion concentrations change substantially. The pump is essential for sustained gradients, not the immediate mechanism for each falling phase of an action potential.
content: TRANSPORT RULE: For one ATP used, the pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, against their concentration gradients.
WHY KEEP PUMPING?: Na+ leaks inward and K+ tends to leak outward. Pumping maintains the gradients that signaling requires.
NOT THE AP SWITCH: Rapid action-potential depolarization and repolarization occur through ion channels, not by the pump instantly moving the voltage up and down.

slides.title: Refractory periods explain recovery and direction
slides.memory: Absolute = absolutely not. Relative = requires more.
slides.source: Book pp. 411–413, 428; C12 L2 slides 13–15; T-A.
slides.notes: Book detail: the absolute refractory period is approximately 0.4–1.0 ms in its example. This is distinct from the whole duration of the action potential. The waveform is an example, not a universal timing rule.
content: ABSOLUTE: From Na+ channel activation until recovery from inactivation: another action potential cannot be triggered in that membrane region.

DIRECTION: The recently active membrane is refractory, helping the normal impulse travel toward excitable membrane ahead.
MAXIMUM FREQUENCY: The absolute refractory period limits how rapidly a neuron can fire again.

slides.memory: Arrival → Calcium → ACh → Receptor → AChE. Calcium triggers release; sodium helps the response.

slides.title: Temporal versus spatial summation
slides.memory: Temporal = time at one place. Spatial = several places at once.
slides.source: Book pp. 425–427; C12 L3 slides 5–6; T-C.
content: TEMPORAL: Repeated input at one synapse arrives close enough in time that a new effect adds to the previous one.
SPATIAL: Inputs from multiple synapses arrive together and combine across locations.
WHAT SUMS?: Graded postsynaptic potentials—not the amplitude of action potentials.
THRESHOLD TEST: The combined effect must sufficiently depolarize the initial segment; inhibitory input may cancel some excitation.

slides.title: Presynaptic inhibition versus facilitation
slides.memory: Less Ca2+ → less release. More Ca2+ → more release.
slides.source: Book p. 427; C12 L3 slide 7; T-C.
slides.notes: Presynaptic means the location relative to the regulated synapse; it should not be reduced to the everyday meaning “something happened earlier in time.”
content: INHIBITION EXAMPLE: An axoaxonic input releases GABA; Ca2+ entry at the target terminal is reduced, so less neurotransmitter is released.
FACILITATION EXAMPLE: An axoaxonic input involving serotonin prolongs/enhances Ca2+ entry, increasing transmitter release.
WHERE IS THE CHANGE?: At the presynaptic terminal before that terminal communicates across its main synapse.
COMPARE WITH IPSP: An IPSP describes the target cell’s graded postsynaptic response. Presynaptic inhibition changes how much transmitter arrives.

slides.title: Conus, cauda and filum: three different things
slides.memory: Conus = cone. Cauda = tail. Filum = thread.
slides.source: Book pp. 436–438; C13 L1 slides 3–8; T-C.
slides.notes: The source explains growth by saying cord growth largely keeps pace to about age four, after which vertebral elongation creates the mismatch. Learn the adult anatomical consequence rather than treating the lecture’s age estimate as a measurement for an individual.

FILUM TERMINALE: Slender supporting strand extending from the conus and contributing to the coccygeal ligament.
WHY THE LONG ROOTS?: The vertebral column grows longer than the cord; lower roots travel downward to their exit sites.

slides.title: Five patterns of neural circuitry
slides.memory: Diverge = distribute. Converge = collect. Serial = sequence. Parallel = simultaneous. Reverberate = repeat.
slides.source: Book pp. 452–453; C13 L3 slide 1; T-D.
slides.notes: The handout text says “Four Patterns” but displays five. The textbook explicitly lists five; all five are included. The lecture uses visual inputs distributed to perception/balance as divergence and multiple balance-related inputs arriving at the cerebellum as convergence.
content: DIVERGENCE / CONVERGENCE: Divergence distributes one input to many outputs. Convergence combines many inputs at one target.
SERIAL / PARALLEL: Serial processing is a sequence of relays. Parallel processing sends information through multiple simultaneous processing pathways.
REVERBERATION: Feedback connections reactivate earlier neurons; activity can continue until inhibition or fatigue ends the loop.
NEURONAL POOL: A functional group of interconnected neurons with particular input sources and output destinations.

slides.title: Stretch reflex: the patellar example
slides.memory: Stretch a muscle → that muscle contracts. The receptor is the muscle spindle.
slides.source: Book pp. 454, 457–458; C13 L3 slide 5.

slides.title: Muscle spindle: intrafusal, extrafusal and gamma
slides.memory: INTRA is IN the spindle; EXTRA is the external working muscle.
slides.source: Book p. 458; C13 L3 slide 8.
slides.notes: Stretching the spindle increases sensory firing and increases stimulation of motor neurons to the same muscle’s extrafusal fibers. Reduced stretch lowers this input. The source uses the example of adding a ball to a partially flexed arm to show adjustment to a new load.

WHY ADJUST?: As a muscle shortens, gamma activity helps keep the sensory region responsive to a newly imposed stretch or load.

slides.title: Withdrawal reflex: flexors on, extensors off
slides.memory: Pull away with flexors; let go with extensors.
slides.source: Book pp. 455, 459–460; C13 L3 slide 4; T-D.
slides.notes: The reflex is polysynaptic. “Reciprocal” means the coordination can work in either direction: activating a muscle group is paired with inhibiting its antagonist. The source calls the limb withdrawal example a flexor reflex.

slides.memory: One leg lifts; the other leg holds.
slides.source: Book pp. 455, 459; C13 L3 slide 6.
slides.notes: Source caution: the handout describes contralateral as a response on both sides. The book defines contralateral as the opposite side; both sides participate when ipsilateral withdrawal and contralateral extension occur together.

slides.title: Polysynaptic responses: the textbook’s five features
slides.memory: Pools, segments, opposites, persistence, cooperation.
slides.notes: The assigned text lists these as five general characteristics: pools of interneurons, more than one segment, reciprocal inhibition, reverberating circuits, and cooperation among reflexes. The slide combines the last two visually but retains all five for recall.

RECIPROCAL INHIBITION: Opposing muscles are coordinated rather than simply contracting together.
REVERBERATION + COOPERATION: Feedback can prolong a response; several reflexes cooperate to produce coordinated movement.

slides.title: The brain can tune a spinal reflex
slides.memory: A spinal reflex is locally organized—not disconnected from the brain.
slides.source: Book pp. 460–461; C13 L3 slide 9.
slides.notes: The book’s Jendrassik example involves interlocking the hands and trying to pull them apart while testing the knee reflex. Learn the concept of reinforcement; reflex interpretation is not a standalone self-diagnosis.
content: LOCAL INITIATION: A spinal reflex does not need a new conscious command before it begins.
DESCENDING INFLUENCE: Brain pathways can facilitate or inhibit spinal interneurons and motor neurons through EPSPs and IPSPs.
REINFORCEMENT: Generalized facilitation enhances a reflex; the book uses the Jendrassik maneuver as an example.
PATTERN REUSE: Higher centers can recruit and adjust existing spinal motor patterns instead of specifying every individual muscle contraction.

slides.memory: Where sources differ, learn the mechanism and retain the source distinction.
content: Multipolar = always motor | Motor examples are multipolar, but interneurons can be multipolar too (Book pp. 394–395).

Adenylate cyclase turns into cAMP | Adenylate cyclase catalyzes ATP conversion to cAMP (p. 424).
Dopamine is an endorphin | Book separates dopamine (amine) from opioid peptides such as endorphins (pp. 420–423).

slides.title: Final teach-back: can you explain the whole route?
slides.memory: The goal is a connected explanation—not a stack of disconnected definitions.
slides.source: Synthesis of Book Chapters 12–13; all six handouts and available transcripts.
content: FROM STIMULUS: Describe a receptor, a graded potential, threshold and the resulting sensory AP.
THROUGH THE CORD: Trace the mixed nerve, dorsal root and spinal integration; distinguish a local reflex from an ascending pathway.
TO THE RESPONSE: Trace motor output through a ventral root, identify an appropriate nerve/effector, and describe the chemical synapse.
IF SOMETHING CHANGES: Predict the effect of blocked Na+ channels, reduced Ca2+ entry, myelin damage, a root lesion or loss of descending inhibition.
